A multimodal MRI-based machine 
learning framework for classifying 
cognitive impairment in cerebral 
small vessel disease
Guihan Lin1,5, Weiyue Chen1,5, Yongkang Geng2,5, Bo Peng3, Surui Liu3, Minjiang Chen1, 
Chunying Pang2, Pengjun Chen1, Chenying Lu1, Zhihan Yan4, Shuiwei Xia1, Yakang Dai3 & 
Jiansong Ji1
The heterogeneity of cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) 
presents a challenge for diagnosis and classification. This study aims to propose a multimodal magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI)-based machine learning framework to effectively classify MCI and NCI in 
CSVD patients. We enrolled 165 CSVD patients, categorized into NCI (n = 81) and MCI (n = 84) groups 
based on neurocognitive assessments. Multimodal MRI data, including T1-weighted, resting-state 
functional MRI, and diffusion tensor images, were collected. Image preprocessing, feature extraction 
and selection were applied to obtain MRI features from three modalities. The AutoGluon platform 
was utilized for model development, and traditional machine learning algorithms were applied for 
comparison. The models were validated using a validation cohort of 83 CSVD patients, and their 
performance was assessed via receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. The AutoGluon model 
to distinguish MCI from NCI based on multimodal MRI features demonstrated high area under the 
curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, balanced accuracy, and F1-score in the training 
cohort (0.926, 88.48%, 88.10%, 88.89%, 89.16%, 88.50%, and 88.63%, respectively) and validation 
cohort (0.878, 81.93%, 86.36%, 76.92%, 80.85%, 81.64%, and 83.51%, respectively). Other traditional 
machine learning models had AUCs of 0.755–0.831, and their prediction accuracies were significantly 
lower than that of AutoGluon model (P < 0.001). Our study provides a multimodal MRI-based machine 
learning framework, utilizing the AutoGluon platform, that outperforms traditional algorithms in 
classifying MCI and NCI, offering a promising tool for the early prediction of MCI in CSVD.
Keywords  Cerebral small vessel disease, Cognitive impairment, Multimodal MRI, Machine learning, 
AutoGluon

Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) encompasses a range of clinical, radiological, and pathological conditions 
resulting from several causes affecting the tiny blood vessels in the brain, including arterioles, capillaries, and 
venules1,2. CSVD was previously disregarded due to the absence of noticeable symptoms, but it is now recognized 
as a significant contributor to vascular cognitive impairment3. It has been suggested that CSVD can cause 
various frontal symptoms, particularly decreased executive and memory functions, by damaging the subcortical 
network4. However, unlike mild cognitive impairment (MCI) related to Alzheimer’s disease, CSVD-related MCI 
(CSVD-MCI) is often overlooked. Moreover, the mechanisms behind cognitive deterioration resulting from 
vascular disease differ from those associated with neurodegenerative disorders5. CSVD-MCI will eventually 
progress to moderate to severe dementia without opportune intervention; thus, detecting cognitive decline early 
is critical for CSVD-MCI prevention and intervention.
According to the latest Vascular Impairment of Cognition Classification Consensus Study guidelines, 
diagnosing MCI generally requires evaluating clinical symptoms, structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 
and neuropsychological assessment6. In practice, a detailed neuropsychological assessment is time-consuming 
and not applicable to all patients, especially those who are illiterate or have aphasia2,7. Even in the most practicable 
settings, these neuropsychological assessments are difficult to administer and must be performed by well-trained 
neurologists; otherwise, there is a risk of misdiagnosis due to inadequate assessment. Indeed, it has been shown 
that the results of neuropsychological assessments such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) vary 
widely due to investigator bias8.
MRI is crucial for diagnosing MCI, particularly for evaluating the structural and functional aspects of the 
brain. This helps determine the extent of CSVD and the likelihood of MCI9,10. In patients with CSVD, structural 
MRI reveals white matter hyperintensities and lacunes, particularly on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated 
inversion recovery images11. However, these imaging markers alone are insufficient for diagnosing cognitive 
impairment because white matter hyperintensities are common in older adults12,13. Therefore, other imaging 
methods are needed to predict and diagnose cognitive decline. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can assess the 
architecture of deep white matter, providing insights into minor alterations potentially associated with MCI14,15. 
In addition, resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) is used to assess the hemodynamics of the brain, allowing for 
the study of functional connectivity (FC)16. However, no studies have directly compared or combined structural 
MRI, DTI, and rs-fMRI in patients with CSVD, and future studies applying multimodal MRI images to predict 
MCI progression in patients with CSVD are needed.
In recent years, machine learning has made significant progress in neuroimaging, greatly promoting the 
automation and intelligent processing of medical images. As an analytical method capable of processing high-
dimensional data, machine learning has been successfully applied to individualized clinical tasks such as 
automatic lesion detection and segmentation, disease classification, risk assessment, and outcome prediction17. 
While machine learning has achieved remarkable results in identifying MCI in patients with CSVD, some 
limitations and challenges still need to be overcome. Firstly, most studies have focused only on using single-
modal imaging data18. Therefore, while many current methods have achieved ideal results in specific tasks, 
they are still insufficient in integrating data from different modalities to assess the complexity of CSVD-related 
cognitive impairment more comprehensively. Secondly, the complexity and high dimensionality of multimodal 
MRI data have significantly increased the difficulty of data processing and model integration, resulting in few 
studies successfully integrating these data into machine learning classifiers to improve prediction performance. 
Thirdly, most studies have relied on traditional machine learning methods, which are highly sensitive to feature 
selection and parameter adjustment, and it is challenging to achieve good generalization capabilities in complex 
scenarios with multimodal and high-dimensional data.
Therefore, in this study, we propose a novel multimodal MRI-based machine learning framework that 
integrates structural, diffusion, and functional MRI data to enhance the classification of CSVD-MCI. By 
leveraging the complementary strengths of these modalities, our framework overcomes the limitations of 
single-modality studies. Using the AutoGluon platform, we automate feature selection and model optimization,

addressing the challenges of traditional machine learning techniques, such as sensitivity to feature selection 
and parameter tuning. These improvements significantly improves classification performance and model 
generalizability, advancing the field by providing a more robust tool for early detection and personalized 
treatment of CSVD-MCI.

Materials and methods
Participants
This study was performed in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration, and approved by the Ethics Committee 
of the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (approval number: 2024-266). For the training 
cohort, patients were recruited from the outpatient and inpatient departments of the Fifth Affiliated Hospital of 
Wenzhou Medical University between September 2019 and January 2024. The inclusion criteria for all patients 
were as follows: (1) aged 50–80  years, (2) able to cooperate in completing all examination items and sign 
informed consent, and (3) a CSVD diagnosis confirmed by imaging examination (see Appendix E1 for details). 
The exclusion criteria for all patients were as follows: (1) a history of brain tumors, head trauma, or surgery; (2) 
cerebral hemorrhage, large-area cerebral infarction, or stenosis of large cerebral blood vessels; (3) the diagnosis 
of other neurological conditions that can cause cognitive impairment, such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s 
disease, or Lewy body dementia, after three years of follow-up; (4) accompanied by severe visual, auditory, or 
language dysfunction; (5) accompanied by mental illness or drug and alcohol abuse; (6) accompanied by serious 
physical diseases, such as heart or liver disease, renal insufficiency, or systemic malignant tumors; and (7) MRI 
contraindications, such as metal dentures, cardiovascular stents, or pacemakers.
According to the cognitive level assessment using neuropsychological scales, the patients were further divided 
into NCI (n = 81) and MCI (n = 84) groups after three years of follow-up. The inclusion criteria for the NCI group 
were as follows: (1) no memory impairment, (2) cognitive performance consistent with their age and education 
level, and (3) a Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) of 0. The inclusion criteria for the MCI group were as follows: 
(1) diagnosed with memory impairment within the past three months, (2) objective memory impairment, (3) a 
CDR of 0.5 despite normal overall cognitive function, and (4) not diagnosed with dementia.
For the validation cohort, patients with CSVD and MCI (n = 44) or NCI (n = 39) were recruited using the 
same inclusion and exclusion criteria between January 2021 and January 2024. The patient recruitment flowchart 
is shown in Fig. 1.

Clinical data collection and neuropsychological scale evaluation
General clinical data, including age, sex, education years, smoking, drinking, hypertension, diabetes, 
hyperlipidemia, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol (TC), and high-density 
lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C), were collected for all patients. Within one week of the MRI scan, two 
experienced neurologists, both of whom were trained in standardized testing procedures, independently 
administered a series of neuropsychological scale assessments. Any discrepancies between their ratings was 
discussed and resolved. The Mini-Mental State Evaluation (MMSE) and MoCA were used to evaluate global 
cognitive function. Additionally, a battery of neuropsychological tests was administered to assess memory, 
language, attention, executive, and visuospatial functions: the Stroop Color Word Test, Auditory Verbal Learning 
Test, Complex Figure Test, Digit Span Test, Clock Drawing Test, and Verbal Fluency Test.
MRI image acquisition

All patients were scanned using a Philips Ingenia CX 3.0 T scanner and a 32-channel head coil. Foam pads were 
placed around the patient’s head to avoid head movement. The scanning parameters were as follows. 3D-T1 
images of the whole brain were obtained using a sagittal three-dimensional magnetization prepared rapid gradient 
echo sequence: repetition time (TR) = 8.464 ms, echo time (TE) = 3.248 ms, field of view (FOV) = 256 × 256 mm, 
flip angle = 12°, matrix = 256 × 256, slice thickness = 1  mm, number of signal averages (NSA) = 1, number of 
slices = 170. rs-fMRI was conducted using a multiband echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence: TR = 2000 ms, 
TE = 30  ms, FOV = 240 × 240  mm, flip angle = 90°, matrix = 64 × 64, slice thickness = 4  mm, gap = 1  mm, 
NSA = 1, number of slices = 40. DTI was acquired using a diffusion-weighted double spin-echo EPI sequence: 
TR = 9000  ms; TE = 85  ms; FOV = 240 × 240  mm; flip angle = 90°; matrix = 128 × 128; slice thickness = 2  mm; 
gap = 1 mm; NSA = 1; number of slices = 74; 64 diffusion-weighted directions with a b of 1000 s/mm2, and 11 
images with a b of 0 s/mm2.
Image preprocessing
The T1 images were preprocessed following a standard procedure19, including (1) resampling images to 
256 × 256 × 256 using a standard template; (2) N3 bias field correction; (3) skull stripping; (4) brain tissue 
segmentation into gray matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid; (5) brain-region labeling according to the 
90-brain-region anatomical automatic labeling (AAL) template20; and (6) cortical reconstruction.
The rs-fMRI images were preprocessed using the Data Processing and Analysis of Brain Imaging (DPABI) 
functional MRI preprocessing toolbox (v8.2, http://rfmri.org/dpabi)21 with the following steps: (1) time points 
were adjusted by removing the first 10, (2) slice timing and motion correction, (3) images were registered to 
the standard Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, (4) images were smoothed with a 4 × 4 × 4 mm3 full 
width at half maximum Gaussian kernel, (5) linear drift was removed and band-pass filtered at 0.01–0.2 Hz, (6) 
covariates were regressed, (7) template matching using the AAL 116-brain-region template, and (8) generation 
of FC matrices.
DTI images were preprocessed using FSL software (v6.0.7, https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/oldwiki/)22 and 
DMRITool software (v0.1.1, https://diffusionmritool.github.io/)23 with the following steps: (1) top-up: 
correcting susceptibility-induced distortions and extracting brain from corrected b0 images using FSL; (2) 
eddy correction24: correcting eddy current-induced distortions and patient motion using FSL to handle high 
b-value DTI images; (3) generating b-value and gradient value text files, fitting the diffusion tensor on eddy-
corrected data; (4) generating masks; (5) extracting matrices to generate fractional anisotropy (FA)25 and mean 
diffusivity (MD)26 maps; (6) computing DTI skeleton images; and (7) constructing brain-region features based 
on a 48-brain-region template.
Feature extraction
We extracted 426 features from the T1 images based on different AAL brain-region templates: 90 from the

segmented gray matter, 90 from the white matter, 90 from the cerebrospinal fluid, 78 from the cortical thickness, 
and 78 from the cortical surface area. In addition, 7134 features were extracted from the rs-fMRI images based 
on 116 AAL brain-region templates: 116 from the ALFF, 116 from the fractional ALFF (fALFF), 116 from the 
ReHo, and 116 from the voxel-mirrored homotopic connectivity images after processing, and 6670 from the 
upper triangular matrix of FC networks based on the AAL 116-brain-region template. Furthermore, 96 features 
were extracted from the DTI images: 48 from the FA and 48 from the MD images based on the Johns Hopkins 
University template. In total, 7656 features were extracted. All features were normalized using the Z-score 
normalization formula (

, where x represents the original feature dataset, x’ represents the normalized 
feature dataset, and μ and σ represent the mean and standard deviation of the original feature dataset.
We repeated the feature extraction process twice on 100 randomly selected patients in two weeks to evaluate 
the intra-observer repeatability, which was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Features 
with ICCs greater than 0.8 were considered to have good reproducibility.
Feature selection
The feature dimensionality was high after feature extraction, which may lead to overfitting if they are inputted 
directly into the classification models. In order to reduce the feature dimensionality, the most discriminative 
features were selected through the following feature selection process. Firstly, an independent samples t-test was 
applied to the feature set, considering a P < 0.05 as statistically significant27. Secondly, after verifying normality 
and performing appropriate transformations when necessary, Pearson’s correlation analysis was performed 
to determine the uniqueness of features, and features with correlation coefficients greater than 0.5 with the

Model construction and evaluation
This study utilized the AutoGluon model29, which automates the entire machine learning process from data 
processing to model training, tuning, and model fusion. Its strengths are its simplicity, robustness, fault tolerance, 
predictions’ predictability, and ability to identify the relevance of features more accurately. The model’s input 
data structure consisted of features from individual modalities (T1 image, rs-fMRI, and DTI) and integrated 
features from all three modalities. AutoGluon can efficiently process high-dimensional data, which is especially 
important for datasets containing features from multiple modalities. On the input feature vector dataset, the 
AutoGluon model trains multiple types of machine learning models on the same data, including SVM, k-
nearest neighbor (KNN), K-means, decision tree (DT), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), RF, extremely 
randomized tree (ET), gradient boosting machine (GBM), categorical boosting (CatBoost), linear regression 
(LR), WeightEnsemble, neural network implemented in PyTorch (NN_TORCH), and neural network with 
FastAI backend (NN_FASTAI) models. These base classifiers are described in Appendix E2, and the parameters 
of the algorithms are listed in Table S1. Through AutoGluon’s automated hyperparameter tuning function, 
we can quickly find the most suitable parameter settings among a large number of candidate models, greatly 
improving the performance of the model and saving a lot of computing and debugging time. The outputs of 
these models are then inputted into a linear model to obtain the final output, which involves weighting the 
outputs using weights determined through training. AutoGluon’s multi-layer stacked integration technique 
significantly improves the accuracy of the models. It ensures that each classifier sees the entire dataset through 
k-fold cross-validation and supports intermediate checkpoints during training, making it possible to recover 
from a checkpoint and continue training even if a failure occurs.
We built the model using the training cohort and calculated the classification performance metrics to evaluate 
the model performance. To ensure the robustness and reliability of the results, we conducted three replicate 
experiments using the above process to validate the model’s generalization ability and assess the consistency 
of the results. The average results of the replicate experiments were used as the final classification performance

metrics. The specific metrics included the AUC, accuracy, sensitivity (recall), specificity, precision, balanced 
accuracy, and F1-score. The formulas used to calculate these quantitative performance metrics are described 
in Appendix E3. The precision-recall (PR) curves of each model were also plotted. To visualize the location of 
brain regions, BrainNet Viewer toolkit (v1.7, https://www.nitrc.org/projects/bnv/) was performed by mapping 
the brain regions in the AAL atlase to the smoothed brain surface. The overall machine learning framework of 
this study is shown in Fig. 2.
Model validation
We used the validation cohort to further validate the model performance. We extracted multimodal MRI 
features from T1-weighted, rs-fMRI, and DTI images using the imaging processing pipeline described above. 
Influential MRI features were selected from multimodal images and inputted into the trained predictive model. 
We conducted two independent samples t-tests on the MRI features to observe their impact in the validation 
cohort. A P-value of > 0.05 indicates that the MRI feature is unreliable for identifying patients with MCI.
Statistical analysis
The statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS (version 26.0; IBM SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The 
normality of all variables was tested using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Normally distributed variables are 
described using means and standard deviations and compared between groups using a t-test. Non-normally 
distributed variables were described using medians and interquartile ranges and compared between groups using 
a Mann–Whitney U-test. Sex, hypertension, and diabetes were compared between groups using a χ2 test. Model 
performance comparisons were conducted using the Delong test, a robust statistical method for distinguishing 
between different models. A two-tailed P-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Demographic characteristics
The training cohort comprised 165 patients with CSVD, 84 with MCI and 81 with NCI. The validation 
cohort comprised 83 patients with CSVD, 44 with MCI and 39 with NCI. The demographic data of training 
and validation cohorts are shown in Table 1. In both cohorts, age, sex, educational years, smoking, drinking, 
hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, LDL-C, TC, and HDL-C did not differ significantly between the patients 
with MCI and those with NCI (all P > 0.05). However, the patients with MCI had significantly lower MMSE 
and MoCA scores than those with NCI in both cohorts (all P < 0.05). Furthermore, the MMSE and MoCA were 
re-administered to the patients in the training cohort at their three-year follow-up. Notably, MMSE and MoCA 
scores did not differ significantly between baseline and the three-year follow-up for patients with MCI and NCI 
(all P > 0.05; Table S2), indicating that the diagnoses were relatively accurate.
Performance of multimodal features
The intra-observer repeatability of the selected features in the training cohort was satisfactory (ICCs = 0.823–
0.976). Table 2 demonstrates the classification performance of the AutoGluon models with different MRI 
features for distinguishing MCI from NCI in the training cohort. The model using only T1-weighted image 
features achieved an AUC of 0.751 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.678–0.815] and an accuracy of 74.55%. 
The model using only rs-fMRI features had an AUC of 0.842 (95% CI 0.778–0.894) and an accuracy of 82.42%. 
And the model using only DTI features had an AUC of 0.807 (95% CI 0.738–0.864) and an accuracy of 76.97%.

Moreover, the model combining features from all modalities achieved the superior performance compared to 
T1 image model (DeLong’s test, P < 0.001), rs-fMRI model (DeLong’s test, P = 0.013), and DTI model (DeLong’s

test, P = 0.003), with an AUC of 0.926 (95% CI 0.875–0.961). Then, we conducted χ2 tests on the accuracy results 
of different models. The combined model had a higher accuracy of 88.48%, compared to T1 image (χ2 = 10.639, 
P = 0.001), rs-fMRI (χ2 = 4.474, P = 0.034), and DTI model (χ2 = 7.656, P = 0.006). Besides, the PR curves also 
illustrate the superior predictive capability of the combined model (Figure S1A). These results demonstrate that 
combining features from multiple MRI modalities improves the classification of patients with MCI and NCI.
Performance of different machine learning models
The different machine learning models were developed using single- and multi-modal MRI features to differentiate 
MCI from NCI, and the ROC curves and AUCs of the different models are shown in Fig. 3. Table 3 shows the 
classification performance of different machine learning models using multimodal MRI features to distinguish 
MCI from NCI. The AutoGluon model outperformed the other models (DeLong’s test, all P < 0.05), achieving 
the highest AUC of 0.926 (95% CI 0.875–0.961). The KNN and DT models also performed well with AUCs of 
0.815 (95% CI 0.745–0.884) and 0.831 (95% CI 0.765–0.896), respectively. However, the SVM, K-means, and RF 
models exhibit relatively lower AUCs of 0.772 (95% CI 0.701–0.844), 0.755 (95% CI 0.680–0.829), 0.768 (95% CI 
0.696–0.840), respectively. Then, we further conducted χ2 tests on the accuracy results of different models. The 
SVM, KNN, DT, K-means, and RF models all had P < 0.001, indicating significant lower accuracies compared to 
the AutoGluon model. And the PR curves also demonstrated the better predictive performance of the AutoGluon 
model (Figure S1B). These results suggest that the proposed AutoGluon model outperforms traditional machine 
learning models in classification accuracy and is particularly effective for leveraging multimodal MRI features to 
classify patients with MCI and NCI.

Feature importance ranking
We utilized the Beware Default Random Forest Importance method to compare the importance of multimodal 
MRI features in classifying patients with MCI and NCI in the training cohort. After analysis, the specific features 
and their corresponding importance values were obtained. The feature importance rankings and corresponding 
weights obtained from the classification of patients with MCI and NCI using the AutoGluon model based on 
multimodal MRI features are shown in Fig. 4. These results indicate the importance of various brain regions in 
the classification task, with the left superior temporal gyrus showing the largest weight, followed by the right 
cuneus region. The weights reflect the significance of each feature’s contribution to the classification outcome, 
with larger weights indicating greater importance. The top ten features in terms of their importance rankings are 
shown in Fig. 5, representing distinct brain regions for T1-weighted, rs-fMRI, and DTI images.
Model validation and evaluation

We further validated the performance of the AutoGluon model based on multimodal MRI features using the 
validation cohort. The features extracted from the validation cohort patients still had good intra-observer 
reproducibility (ICC = 0.811–0.935). The AutoGluon model classified patients with MCI and NCI with an AUC

Discussion
This study aimed to develop an effective and accessible model to meet the critical clinical need of early 
identification of CSVD-related MCI. To this end, we compiled a comprehensive dataset, including clinical 
assessments, neuropsychological evaluations, and multimodal MRI data from CSVD patients who were followed 
for three years. Using a data-driven approach with the AutoGluon platform, we integrated features from three

MRI modalities (T1-weighted, rs-fMRI and DTI) for the first time, and developed AutoGluon automated 
machine learning model, which yielded the highest classification performance among the models tested. Our 
model relies on MRI protocols routinely used in clinical diagnostics for suspected cognitive impairment in 
CSVD, aligning with established imaging guidelines. During validation with an independent cohort, the model 
maintained high AUC and accuracy, confirming its generalizability and robustness in identifying CSVD patients 
at high risk of MCI.
Based on the feature importance ranking results, some brain regions were more important in distinguishing 
MCI and NCI in patients with CSVD. Specifically, the left superior temporal gyrus and right cuneus had larger 
weights in the classification task, indicating their significance in the pathophysiology of MCI. These findings 
provide important insights into the pathological mechanisms of CSVD. The relationship of the left superior 
temporal gyrus and the right cuneus with MCI has garnered considerable attention. Some studies indicate that 
patients with MCI often exhibit structural and functional abnormalities in the left superior temporal gyrus and 
right cuneus regions30. Alterations in the left superior temporal gyrus and right cuneus in patients with MCI 
are closely associated with cognitive decline31. These brain regions are closely linked with cognitive functions 
such as language, memory, and executive function, and their structural and functional abnormalities may lead

to cognitive impairment and other symptoms in patients with MCI.
The pathophysiological mechanisms of the abnormalities in the left superior temporal gyrus and right 
cuneus may be related to various factors, including microvascular changes, white matter damage, and neuronal 
loss. Specific vascular pathologies, such as microinfarcts and hypoperfusion, are key contributors to these 
abnormalities. Wardlaw et al.32 indicated that patients with CSVD often exhibit microvascular alterations, including 
microvascular spasm, microaneurysms, and microvascular rupture, leading to local cerebral hypoperfusion and

subsequent ischemia and microinfarction in brain tissues, thereby exacerbating the abnormalities in the left 
superior temporal gyrus. These microinfarcts disrupt both gray and white matter structures, impairing neural 
networks and contributing to cognitive decline. Pantoni et al.33 demonstrated that long-standing hypertension 
can cause arteriolosclerosis and narrowing of small arteries in the cerebral white matter, resulting in impaired 
white matter perfusion, accelerated demyelination, and death of white matter neurons, thus contributing to 
white matter damage in the right cuneus. Chronic hypoperfusion and ischemia, in turn, worsen these processes, 
leading to persistent neuronal dysfunction. Cannistraro et al.2 found that patients with CSVD often exhibit 
neuronal loss and brain tissue atrophy, which may be associated with chronic cerebral ischemia, hypoxia, and 
neuronal intolerance to ischemia and microinfarcts. These pathological changes, including microinfarcts, may 
lead to apoptosis and loss of neurons in the right cuneus, affecting its function and structure. In addition, 
hypoperfusion is commonly observed in CSVD, leading to insufficient oxygen supply to critical brain regions, 
including the right cuneus. In patients with MCI, the affected regions, including the superior temporal gyrus 
and cuneus, may also be influenced by factors such as vascular inflammation, microcirculatory disorders, and 
neuroinflammation, leading to additional cellular damage, synaptic disruption, and functional impairment, 
further exacerbating cognitive decline. Therefore, the left superior temporal gyrus and right cuneus may play 
crucial roles in the pathogenesis of MCI, and further research is warranted to gain a deeper understanding of 
the mechanisms underlying their involvement, which could ultimately provide more effective approaches for the 
early diagnosis and treatment of MCI.
Our study introduced a multimodal MRI-based machine learning model, leveraging the AutoGluon platform, 
to distinguish between MCI and NCI in CSVD patients through a comprehensive analysis of T1-weighted, rs-
fMRI, and DTI features. This integrative approach enabled an in-depth evaluation of structural, functional, and 
microstructural brain characteristics, overcoming the limitations of a single MRI modality in comprehensively 
capturing pathological changes. The multimodal fusion model achieved an accuracy of 88.48% and an AUC of 
0.926 in distinguishing MCI from NCI in the training cohort, outperforming traditional models based on a single 
MRI modality in classifying CSVD-related cognitive impairment. In addition, the automatic feature selection

and model tuning capabilities in AutoGluon further enhanced the classification accuracy and adaptability of the 
framework. When validated on an independent cohort, the model demonstrated a robust accuracy of 81.93% 
and maintained high AUC (0.878), sensitivity (86.36%), and specificity (76.92%), underscoring its potential 
applicability in early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies for CSVD. In our study, early diagnosis 
of MCI through multimodal MRI data enables clinicians to identify subtle brain changes in CSVD patients 
before cognitive decline becomes clinically detectable. By integrating multiple imaging modalities with machine 
learning, our framework further improves the accuracy of MCI classification, supports personalized treatment 
strategies, and enhances clinical decision-making, especially in resource-limited settings.
This study had several limitations. Firstly, as a retrospective study, it is susceptible to selection bias, which 
may limit its generalizability. In order to address this, future prospective studies should include larger, more 
diverse patient cohorts to improve their model’s robustness across different populations. Secondly, its relatively 
small sample size limits the statistical power. Future studies should incorporate larger datasets to ensure their 
model’s broader applicability, and the application of bootstrapping techniques are needed to ensure statistical 
robustness. Thirdly, while our model was internally validated, it lacks external independent testing, which is 
crucial for confirming its generalizability in clinical settings. Future studies should focus on external validation 
using independent cohorts. Fourth, it utilized only three MRI modalities (T1-weighted, rs-fMRI, DTI) and did 
not incorporate other potentially valuable imaging modalities, such as arterial spin labeling or susceptibility-
weighted imaging, potentially limiting its broader clinical applicability. Future studies should incorporate more 
imaging modalities to enhance the model’s diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility. Lastly, the reliability of rs-
fMRI features in the validation cohort was relatively lower, which could be attributed to patient characteristics, 
differences in scan quality, or the increased sensitivity of functional connectivity measures to subtle brain activity 
changes, leading to less consistency across cohorts. Future research should focus on improving the reliability of 
rs-fMRI features by using larger sample sizes and advanced preprocessing techniques, and exploring subgroup 
analyses to better understand these inconsistencies. In addition, cross-validation or external validation methods 
can be considered to further improve the reliability of feature selection.
Conclusions
This study enhances understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying cognitive decline in patients 
with CSVD by revealing the relationship between multimodal MRI features and MCI from anatomical, 
microstructural, and functional perspectives. We used the AutoGluon platform to construct a novel machine 
learning model based on multimodal MRI features to distinguish between MCI and NCI in patients with CSVD. 
The proposed model represents a valuable tool for early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies, which 
could help guide clinical decision-making and improve the prognosis of patients with CSVD with cognitive 
impairment.
